tutorial.title: Error Boundaries
tutorial.seoTitle: React Error Boundaries Tutorial: Catching Render Errors

questions.question: What happens when a render error is not caught by any boundary?
options: Only the failing component is removed
React unmounts the entire component tree
The error is logged and ignored
questions.explanation: Since React 16 an uncaught render error unmounts the whole tree, on the grounds that a corrupted interface is more dangerous than none.

questions.question: How do you create an error boundary?
options: With a class component implementing getDerivedStateFromError and/or componentDidCatch
questions.explanation: There is still no hook equivalent. Boundaries are class components, though libraries such as react-error-boundary wrap that in a friendlier API.

questions.question: Which method should contain logging to an error reporting service?
options: componentDidCatch, because it runs after the commit and side effects are allowed
questions.explanation: `getDerivedStateFromError` runs during rendering and must stay pure. `componentDidCatch` runs after the commit and receives the component stack.

questions.question: Which of these will an error boundary NOT catch?
options: An error thrown while rendering a child
An error in a child's constructor
An error thrown inside an onClick handler
An error in a child's render method
questions.explanation: Event handlers run outside the render cycle. Use try/catch and put the failure into state yourself.

questions.question: How can an async error reach an error boundary?
options: Catch it, store it in state, and throw it during the next render
Use componentDidCatch with an async keyword
questions.explanation: Throwing during render is the only thing a boundary sees, so `if (error) throw error;` after `.catch(setError)` routes it there.

questions.question: What happens if a boundary's own fallback throws?
options: The error propagates to the next boundary above it
questions.explanation: A boundary cannot catch itself, which is why fallbacks should be plain and never depend on the shape of the error data.

questions.question: Why place a boundary around each independent widget?
options: So one widget failing does not remove the rest of the page
questions.explanation: Granular boundaries contain the blast radius: a broken chart leaves the rest of the dashboard usable.

questions.question: In what order should Suspense and an error boundary be nested?
questions.explanation: The error boundary goes outside so it can catch failures from the lazy chunk or the data read that the Suspense boundary is waiting on.
